title: Reading a Privacy Notice in Five Minutes
body:
Reading a privacy notice in five minutes means finding the answers that matter without reading every clause. The five answers are: what data is collected, why it is collected, who else receives it, how long it is kept, and how to contact the service about it. Most notices hide these answers in headings, so the skill is scanning headings first and reading only the sections that answer the five questions.

Nobody reads every notice, which is why a five-minute method beats a perfect method nobody uses.

The working method is five-minute privacy-notice reading. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Scan headings for collection, purpose, sharing, retention, and contact
  2. Note what data is collected beyond what the service needs
  3. Note who else receives data and for what purpose
  4. Note how long data is kept and how deletion is requested
  5. Decide whether the answers are acceptable before signing up

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Collection answer found; OK :: Purpose answer found; OK :: Sharing answer found; OK :: Retention and deletion answers found; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. A five-minute reading is a screening method, not legal analysis, and it cannot interpret any notice's legal meaning. Where a notice governs sensitive data or a child's data, a fuller reading, or professional advice, is warranted, and this record does not offer legal advice. A common mistake is accepting a notice unread because it is long, which is exactly what its length is designed to encourage. title: Browser Privacy Settings Check
body:
A browser privacy settings check walks through the browser's privacy section and sets it deliberately: cookies, site data, tracking protection, location, camera, microphone, and notifications. The check also covers clearing site data on exit where offered and reviewing which sites have standing permissions. Browsers differ in wording, but every major browser offers the same families of controls, so the check teaches families, not menu paths.

The browser is the room where most tracking happens, and its settings are the room's doors and windows.

The working method is browser privacy-settings check. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Open privacy settings and read each section before changing anything
  2. Set cookie and site-data handling to the strictest comfortable level
  3. Turn on tracking protection where offered
  4. Review site permissions for location, camera, microphone, and notifications
  5. Clear site data on exit where the option exists and fits your use

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Privacy sections read; OK :: Cookie handling set deliberately; OK :: Tracking protection on; OK :: Site permissions reviewed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Stricter settings can break some sites, which then need a per-site exception, and this record treats that friction honestly rather than promising a free lunch. It does not cover any particular browser's features, which change with versions. A common mistake is changing one switch and assuming the browser is private, since controls live in several sections. title: Cookie Choices: Accept, Reject, Manage
body:
Cookie choices appear as banners asking to accept all, reject, or manage cookies, and the safe habit is to choose reject or manage rather than accept all by reflex. Cookies are small pieces of data sites store in the browser, and while some are needed for a site to work, many exist to track visits across sites for advertising. Managing choices means allowing necessary cookies, refusing tracking cookies where the choice exists, and clearing cookies periodically.

Accept-all is the fastest click and the broadest permission, which is why banners are designed to make it the easiest.

The working method is cookie-choice handling. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose reject or manage on cookie banners, not accept-all by reflex
  2. Allow necessary cookies and refuse tracking cookies where offered
  3. Clear cookies periodically, especially after sensitive browsing
  4. Use the browser's site-data settings to block third-party cookies where offered
  5. Revisit cookie choices after a site redesign, which sometimes resets them

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Reject or manage chosen over accept-all; OK :: Necessary cookies allowed, tracking refused; OK :: Cookies cleared periodically; OK :: Third-party cookies blocked where offered; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Cookie controls differ between sites and regions, and some sites limit features when tracking cookies are refused, which this record notes honestly. It does not cover the legal status of any banner, which varies by jurisdiction. A common mistake is clicking accept-all to dismiss the banner, which grants the broadest permission to stop an annoyance. title: Location Permissions Audit
body:
A location permissions audit reviews which apps may know where a device is, and when. Location is among the most revealing data a phone holds, since it shows home, work, school, routines, and travel. The audit sets most apps to never, a few to only while in use, and almost none to always, and it removes location from photos shared publicly where the device offers that choice.

A location history is a diary written without words, and diaries deserve locked drawers.

The working method is location-permission audit. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every app with location permission on the device
  2. Set most apps to never and a few to only while in use
  3. Set almost no app to always, and justify each exception
  4. Remove location from shared photos where the device offers it
  5. Repeat the audit after installing new apps

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Apps with location listed; OK :: Most apps set to never; OK :: Always grants justified individually; OK :: Photo location removed for sharing; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Some apps genuinely need location while in use, such as navigation, and this record does not suggest breaking them. It teaches the audit pattern, and where an app refuses to work without always location, the audit's answer is to weigh that cost openly. A common mistake is granting always location to an app that needs it once, and then forgetting the grant forever. title: App Permissions Audit
body:
An app permissions audit reviews what each installed app may access: contacts, photos, microphone, camera, files, and more. The rule for each permission is whether the app's job needs it: a photo app needs photos, but a flashlight does not need contacts. The audit removes permissions that fail the job test, uninstalls apps that are unused, and repeats after updates, which sometimes add new permission requests.

Permissions granted at install are forgotten within days, while the access they grant lasts until it is removed.

The working method is app-permission audit. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List installed apps and their permissions
  2. Test each permission against whether the app's job needs it
  3. Remove permissions that fail the job test
  4. Uninstall apps that are unused
  5. Repeat the audit after major updates

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Apps and permissions listed; OK :: Job test applied to each permission; OK :: Failing permissions removed; OK :: Unused apps uninstalled; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Permission names and controls differ between systems, so this record teaches the job test rather than naming menu paths. It does not cover system-level permissions that cannot be changed, which the device maker controls. A common mistake is granting every permission an app requests at install to reach the app faster. title: Ad Personalization Switches
body:
Ad personalization switches are the controls that decide whether advertising shown to a user is tailored from their activity. The switches live in device settings, browser settings, and individual ad accounts, and turning them off does not remove advertising, but changes it from tailored to general. The review covers the device ad setting, the browser ad setting, and the largest ad accounts the user actually uses.

Turning off personalization does not end ads, and promising otherwise would be dishonest; it changes what the ads are based on.

The working method is ad-personalization switch review. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the device-level ad personalization setting and set it deliberately
  2. Find the browser-level ad setting and set it deliberately
  3. Review ad settings in the ad accounts actually used
  4. Understand that general ads will replace tailored ads, not no ads
  5. Repeat the review after device or account changes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Device ad setting set deliberately; OK :: Browser ad setting set deliberately; OK :: Ad account settings reviewed; OK :: General ads expected, not no ads; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Ad systems differ and change, and some tailored advertising continues through channels these switches do not govern, such as contextual ads based on the page itself. This record teaches the switch review, not a promise of ad-free browsing. A common mistake is believing that turning off personalization removes advertising, and then distrusting the controls when ads continue. title: Tracker Blocking Basics
body:
Tracker blocking basics cover the tools that reduce cross-site tracking: browsers and extensions that block known trackers, private browsing modes that discard site data on close, and search tools that do not profile queries. Blocking is not invisibility: a site still sees the visit itself, and blocking can break site features that depend on third-party content. The honest promise of blocking is less tracking, not no tracking.

Trackers are the quiet passengers on most pages, and blocking is how a reader leaves them at the door.

The working method is tracker-blocking basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use a browser or extension that blocks known trackers
  2. Use private browsing for sessions that should not persist
  3. Prefer search tools that do not profile queries where possible
  4. Allow a broken site's trackers only as a per-site exception, not globally
  5. Combine blocking with cookie and permission habits, since no single tool suffices

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Tracker blocking in use; OK :: Private browsing used for sensitive sessions; OK :: Per-site exceptions only, never global; OK :: Blocking combined with cookie habits; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Blocking tools differ in what they block and how they are funded, and this record does not recommend any particular tool. It teaches the combination habit, since blocking, cookies, and permissions together protect more than any one alone. A common mistake is installing a blocker and assuming invisibility, then sharing sensitive details without restraint on the strength of it. title: Fingerprinting in Plain Language
body:
Fingerprinting in plain language is identification without cookies: a site collects many small details about a browser and device, such as screen size, fonts, and settings, and the combination is often unique enough to recognize the same visitor again. Because no cookie is stored, clearing cookies does not defeat it. The defenses are partial: browsers that standardize these details, extensions that randomize them, and the habit of not treating cookie clearing as complete privacy.

Fingerprinting works because a browser's details, taken together, are as distinctive as a face in a crowd.

The working method is browser fingerprinting explained and limited. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Learn what fingerprinting collects: many small browser and device details
  2. Understand that clearing cookies does not defeat fingerprinting
  3. Use a browser that standardizes fingerprint details where possible
  4. Avoid installing unusual fonts and extensions that increase uniqueness
  5. Treat fingerprint defenses as partial, and combine them with other habits

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Fingerprinting concept understood; OK :: Cookie clearing not mistaken for full privacy; OK :: Standardizing browser in use where possible; OK :: Unusual uniqueness-increasing additions avoided; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Fingerprinting defenses are an arms race, and no record here promises unrecognizability. This record teaches the concept and the partial defenses honestly, and it does not cover fingerprinting for security purposes, such as fraud detection, which is a different use of similar techniques. A common mistake is believing that clearing cookies makes a browser unrecognizable, while its fingerprint remains. title: Access Request: Asking for Your Data
body:
An access request asks a service to show the personal data it holds about the requester. The request is a short, polite letter or form submission stating who you are, what you are asking for, and how you wish to receive it, with proof of identity attached only as the service requires. Keeping a copy of the request and the date sent matters, because deadlines and follow-ups depend on it, and this record's template habits keep the copy safe.

People cannot control data they cannot see, which is why access is the first right in practice, even where it is not the first in law.

The working method is data-access request drafting. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Identify the service and its published data-request contact or form
  2. Write a short request stating identity, scope, and preferred format
  3. Attach only the proof of identity the service requires
  4. Keep a copy of the request and the date sent
  5. Diary a follow-up date and escalate politely if no reply arrives

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Request contact or form found; OK :: Scoped request written; OK :: Proof of identity limited to what is required; OK :: Copy and date kept; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Access rights, deadlines, and exceptions vary by jurisdiction and by service, and this record does not offer legal advice about any particular request. It teaches the drafting and record-keeping habits that make any request stronger. A common mistake is sending a vague request for everything, which invites delay, instead of a scoped request that can be answered. title: Correction Request: Fixing Wrong Data
body:
A correction request asks a service to fix personal data that is wrong, incomplete, or out of date. The request states what is wrong, what the correct value is, and what evidence supports the correction, in a short letter that a reviewer can act on without further correspondence. Keeping a copy and the evidence matters, because a correction refused without reason can be challenged, and the challenge needs the paper trail.

Wrong data harms quietly, through decisions made on it that the person never sees.

The working method is data-correction request drafting. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Identify the wrong value and the correct value precisely
  2. Gather the evidence that supports the correction
  3. Write a short request stating the error, the correction, and the evidence
  4. Keep a copy of the request, the evidence, and the date sent
  5. Diary a follow-up and keep the service's reply with the request

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Wrong and correct values stated precisely; OK :: Supporting evidence gathered; OK :: Short actionable request written; OK :: Copy, evidence, and date kept; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Correction rights and exceptions vary by jurisdiction, and some data, such as opinions or historical records, may not be correctable in the way a person hopes. This record does not offer legal advice, and it teaches the drafting habit, not any particular legal outcome. A common mistake is complaining generally that data is wrong without stating the correct value, which gives the reviewer nothing to change. title: Deletion Request: Asking for Erasure
body:
A deletion request asks a service to erase personal data it holds, and it is the most consequential data-rights request, because erasure cannot easily be undone. The request states which data or account is to be erased, confirms the requester's understanding of what will be lost, and is sent through the service's published channel. Before sending, the requester should export anything they wish to keep, since deletion and export are companion steps, not alternatives.

Deletion is a door that locks behind you, so the export must happen before the request, not after.

The working method is data-deletion request drafting. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Decide precisely which data or account is to be erased
  2. Export anything to be kept before requesting deletion
  3. Send the request through the service's published channel
  4. Confirm understanding of what will be lost, in the request itself
  5. Keep a copy of the request and the service's confirmation

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Scope of erasure decided precisely; OK :: Export completed before requesting; OK :: Request sent through published channel; OK :: Confirmation kept; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Deletion rights have exceptions, such as data a service must keep by law or for ongoing disputes, and this record does not promise complete erasure from every system. A later record covers backups and copies, which are the honest limit of any deletion request. A common mistake is requesting deletion before exporting, and then discovering the only copy is gone. title: Deletion Across Backups and Copies
body:
Deletion across backups and copies is the honest limit of any erasure request: a service may hold data in live systems, backups, logs, and processors' systems, and each copy has its own deletion rhythm. Backups are often overwritten on a cycle rather than edited, so a deleted record may persist in a backup until that backup ages out. The requester's tools are: asking what copies exist, asking when backups cycle, requesting confirmation for each system, and following up after the stated cycle.

Live deletion is instant, but backup deletion is a calendar, and confusing the two breeds false confidence.

The working method is deletion across backups, copies, and processors. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ask the service which systems hold copies of the data
  2. Ask when backups cycle and when the data will age out
  3. Request confirmation for live systems separately from backups
  4. Diary a follow-up after the stated backup cycle
  5. Keep the service's answers with the original request

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Copy systems asked about; OK :: Backup cycle asked about; OK :: Live and backup confirmations separated; OK :: Follow-up diarized after the cycle; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Some copies may lawfully persist, and some processors may hold data under their own terms, which this record does not pretend to override. It teaches the questions and the follow-up rhythm that make deletion verifiable rather than merely promised. A common mistake is accepting a live-deletion confirmation as proof that every backup copy is gone too. title: Portability: Taking Your Data Elsewhere
body:
Portability means taking your data from one service to another in a usable form, rather than starting over. The practice is: find the export tool, download the export, check that it opens and contains what was expected, store it safely, and only then import it elsewhere or close the old account. An export that cannot be opened or is missing key data is a failed portability attempt, and the failure should be reported before the old account is closed.

Data you cannot take with you is data you are renting, not data you own in any practical sense.

The working method is data-portability export and transfer. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the service's export tool and its format
  2. Download the export and store it safely
  3. Open the export and check it contains what was expected
  4. Import elsewhere or keep the export as an archive
  5. Report a failed or incomplete export before closing the old account

The output reads: OK :: Export tool and format found; OK :: Export downloaded and stored safely; OK :: Export opened and checked; OK :: Failure reported before closing old account; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. A common mistake is closing the old account before checking that the export opens and is complete. title: Objecting to Processing and Marketing
body:
Objecting to processing and marketing is the right to say no to particular uses of personal data, most commonly direct marketing and certain profiling. The practice is: find the objection or opt-out control, use it, keep the confirmation, and check whether marketing stops within the stated period. Where marketing continues, the confirmation and the dates become the evidence for a follow-up complaint, which is why the paper trail matters as much as the click.

An objection without a kept confirmation is a claim without evidence when marketing continues.

The working method is objection to processing and marketing. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Find the objection or opt-out control for the use in question
  2. Use it and note the date and the stated effect period
  3. Keep the confirmation with the date
  4. Check whether the use stops within the stated period
  5. Follow up with the confirmation and dates if it does not

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Objection control found; OK :: Objection used and dated; OK :: Confirmation kept; OK :: Effect checked within stated period; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Use and limits. Objection rights and their exceptions vary by jurisdiction, and some processing, such as that needed to perform a contract or meet a legal duty, may continue despite an objection. This record does not offer legal advice about any particular objection. A common mistake is opting out and deleting the confirmation, leaving nothing to show when the use continues. title: Consent Records: Keeping Your Own Log
body:
Consent records kept by the user are a private log of every permission granted: which service, what data, when, for what purpose, and when consent was withdrawn. Services keep their own logs, but a user's own log is independent evidence when memories differ, and it is the tool that turns a vague feeling of oversharing into a list that can be pruned. The log can be paper or a simple file, and its only requirement is that it is kept in one place and reviewed.

A permission nobody wrote down is a permission nobody will remember to withdraw.

The working method is personal consent log keeping. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Record each consent: service, data, date, purpose
  2. Record each withdrawal with its date and confirmation
  3. Keep the log in one place, paper or file
  4. Review the log quarterly and prune stale consents
  5. Use the log to draft access, correction, and deletion requests

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Consents recorded with service, data, date, purpose; OK :: Withdrawals recorded with confirmations; OK :: Log kept in one place; OK :: Log reviewed quarterly; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. A personal log does not override a service's records or any legal frame, and it is evidence for the user, not a legal instrument. It does not cover consent given on behalf of children or others, which needs its own care. A common mistake is keeping consents in scattered emails and messages, which is the same as keeping no log at all. title: Privacy Audit Routine
body:
A privacy audit routine is a quarterly walk through the whole toolkit in one sitting: browser settings, app permissions, location grants, cookie choices, ad switches, tracker blocking, consent log, and pending data requests. Done quarterly, it catches drift: the permission granted for one trip, the cookie choice reset by a redesign, the request whose follow-up date passed unnoticed. The audit ends by setting the next audit date, because an audit without a next date is a one-time event, not a routine.

Privacy decays by drift, and only a scheduled audit notices drift.

The working method is quarterly privacy audit routine. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Walk browser, app, and location settings in one sitting
  2. Review cookie choices, ad switches, and tracker blocking
  3. Review the consent log and prune stale consents
  4. Check pending data requests and their follow-up dates
  5. Set the next audit date before finishing

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Browser, app, and location walked; OK :: Cookies, ads, and trackers reviewed; OK :: Consent log pruned; OK :: Next audit date set; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. An audit is a snapshot, and a permission granted the week after escapes notice until the next one. The record therefore pairs the quarterly audit with the habit of reviewing permissions whenever a new app is installed. A common mistake is auditing only the browser and calling privacy done, while apps and consents drift unexamined.
